summary: This memo updates RFC 4733 by adding event codes for modem, fax and text telephony signals carried in the telephony event RTP payload. It supersedes the assignment of such codes in RFC 2833, obsoleting that part of it.

plainLanguage.summary: Besides keypad beeps, old fax and modem machines make their own special sounds. This gives names to those sounds so they can be sent as small messages too.

questions: what are rtp telephone events for fax and modem
what is the difference between v.8 and v.8 bis
subtitle: Event codes that let VoIP gateways report fax, modem and text-phone signals as small RTP events.

tldr.problem: Gateways that bridge fax machines, modems and text telephones across an IP network need a quick, reliable way to tell each other about the control tones and signals that start, change and end those sessions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4734 defines named telephony events for those signals (such as V.8 bis, V.21, V.8, V.25, V.32, T.30 and text-telephony indicators), with event codes, to be carried in the RFC 4733 telephone-event RTP payload.
tldr.outcome: It supersedes the data-related event codes of RFC 2833 and registers its codes in the RFC 4733 registry. The actual fax, modem or text content travels in other payload types.

today: RFC 4734 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2006. It obsoletes the corresponding part of RFC 2833 and updates RFC 4733, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 4734 extends the telephony events of RFC 4733 to cover the control events and tones that can appear on a line serving a fax machine, a modem or a text telephony device. The events are grouped by the ITU-T Recommendation that defines them. Their purpose is to support negotiation, start-up and takedown of fax, modem or text sessions, and transitions between operating modes.

The events do not carry the payload. The actual fax, modem or text data typically travels in other payload types, such as V.150.1 modem relay, voice-band data, Clearmode, T.38 for fax or RFC 4103 for text. The RFC warns implementers not to rely on its descriptions of the modem protocols without consulting the ITU-T originals.

The typical use is a pair of gateways bridging PSTN terminals. Each gateway is both sender and receiver, events must be reported early so playout is timely, they must be played in order, and transfer must be reliable. Echo suppressors and cancellers may re-activate after as little as 100 ms of no signal, so tone events must be reported quickly.
sections.plainLanguage: Two fax machines talk across the internet through helper boxes at each end. The boxes say which beep just happened so the other box can repeat it on time.

sections.title: Start-Up Tones: V.8 bis, V.8, V.25 and V.32
sections.content:
V.8 bis signals are two tone segments. The first is a dual-frequency tone held for 400 ms (events V8bISeg and V8bRSeg); the second is a single tone held for 100 ms that says which of six signals it is (CRdSeg, CReSeg, MRdSeg, MReSeg, ESiSeg, ESrSeg). No events are defined for V.8 bis messages, which may be sent as V.21 bit events.

V.8 is an older negotiation in which only the calling terminal chooses the mode. The RFC defines ANSam, /ANSam (after a phase reversal, which recurs every 450 ms) and CI events. A receiver of /ANSam MUST reverse the tone phase at the start of playout and every 450 ms after.

V.25 uses a calling tone (CT, 1300 Hz bursts) and an answer tone (ANS and /ANS, 2100 Hz). For V.32/V.32bis, V32AA and V32AC report the calling and answering bit patterns, and SHOULD be reported as soon as detected.

Each group has a congestion note. V.8 bis tolerates little delay, while V.8 is mostly robust and V.25 can have tone playout extended.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two modems chat they trade secret hello beeps, like a knock pattern on a clubhouse door. Each knock has a name here so it can be passed along quickly.

sections.title: V.21 Bit Events
sections.content:
V.21 is a modem protocol with a maximum rate of 300 bits/s and two channels. Other protocols (V.8 bis, V.18, T.30) use it for control data. The RFC defines four events, one for each combination of channel and bit value: codes 37 to 40.

Senders SHOULD report a completed event for every bit sent rather than at 0/1 transitions, SHOULD pack several events into one packet (eight to ten bits is a reasonable interval) and SHOULD carry the retransmitted events using RFC 2198 redundancy. At 300 bits/s one bit lasts 3.33 ms, which is 26.67 timestamp units at 8000 Hz, so durations alternate between 26 and 27 units and senders MUST derive them as differences between event start times so events never overlap.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine sending a message by flicking a light on and off. Each flick is a tiny event. Because the flicks are so quick, the helper boxes bundle many into one envelope.

sections.title: Fax Events from T.30
sections.content:
T.30 governs Group III fax terminals. The calling terminal sends CNG, a 1100-Hz tone in bursts of 0.5 s on and 3 s off. The called terminal may answer with CED, which is physically identical to V.25 ANS and shares codes 32 and 33 (with /CED), or with V.8 ANSam. A V.21 preamble flag event (code 54) marks the run of HDLC flags that precedes each message.

Fax negotiation messages (DIS, DTC, DCS, CFR) are sent as V.21 at 300 bits/s. They may be reported as V.21 bit events or in another payload type. If sent as bit events, the information MUST be complete, including HDLC flags, checksum and the extra '0' bits inserted to avoid false flags.
sections.plainLanguage: A fax machine first sings a short beep every few seconds that means a fax is calling. The other machine answers with a steady beep, then they swap notes on how to send the pages.

sections.title: Text Telephony and a Generic Indicator
sections.content:
Legacy text telephones use many modem types. The RFC recommends that gateways convert text carried by legacy modem protocols into RFC 4103 packets. Gateways that can only pass it as voice-band data can use indicator events to tell the receiver what kind of content it is. They are ANS2225, V21L110, V21L300, V21H300, B103L300, V23Main, V23Back, Baud4545, Baud50 and XCIMark.

For all but ANS2225, the sender SHOULD report as soon as the content is recognized and SHOULD retransmit that initial report twice at short intervals (20 ms is suggested). If the content type changes, it MUST send a report for the new type. Indicators are assumed to accompany the main media, for example G.711 voice-band data in an RFC 2198 redundancy payload.

A single generic event, VBDGen (code 61), flags a modem of unidentified type. It SHOULD NOT be sent if a more specific event is available.
sections.plainLanguage: Old text phones each use their own funny sounds. These events are like labels on a package saying what kind of sound is inside, so the receiver knows how to handle it.

sections.title: Combining Events with Other Payloads
sections.content:
Gateways could negotiate every possible payload type at call start, but that over-allocates resources. Instead, named events can buy time while out-of-band signaling moves the session to a new payload type. This works for sessions that begin with V.8, V.8 bis, T.30 or V.25 control sequences. Receiving gateways MUST be prepared to switch payload type within the time constraints of the application. Several procedures leave 75 ms of silence between control signaling and data.

One strategy is to send the telephone-event and the data payload together in an RFC 2198 redundancy arrangement. The data payload and the events MUST then cover exactly the same content and time period, or spurious events appear downstream. Section 4 of the RFC walks through an example V.8 negotiation for V.34 modem start-up with a 30 ms event packetization interval.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper boxes can send both a note that says the beep happened and the real sound, in one package. The two have to match, or the other box gets confused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
V.21 bit events may carry user-sensitive data such as log-on sequences, so the attacks of concern include password sniffing, session hijacking by message insertion, man-in-the-middle modification and denial of service. Transmission of V.21 bit events MUST be given confidentiality protection, and message authentication and integrity protection MUST also be provided.

The other events used only for setup and control do not expose user data, but disclosure could reveal equipment capabilities. Confidentiality protection SHOULD be provided, and authentication and integrity protection MUST be provided to meet the injection threat. SRTP (RFC 3711) meets these requirements and SHOULD be used.
sections.plainLanguage: These beeps can sometimes carry private messages, so they should be sent in a locked box, and the receiver should check nobody tampered with them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC adds its events to the registry established by RFC 4733. The codes assigned run from 23 to 29, 30 to 40, 49, and 52 to 63, with this RFC as the reference. Some share a code on purpose: ESiSeg uses 38 like the V.21 channel 1 '1' bit, and ESrSeg uses 40 like the channel 2 '1' bit, because they use the same frequencies. ANS and CED share 32, and /ANS and /CED share 33.
sections.plainLanguage: Every beep gets its own number in a shared phone book of beeps, so everyone looks up the same number for the same sound.

viz.caption: SELECTED EVENT CODES ADDED TO THE RFC 4733 REGISTRY (RFC 4734)

items.label: CRdSeg
items.desc: Second segment of V.8 bis CRd signal.

items.label: CReSeg
items.desc: Second segment of V.8 bis CRe signal.

items.label: MRdSeg
items.desc: Second segment of V.8 bis MRd signal.

items.label: MReSeg
items.desc: Second segment of V.8 bis MRe signal.

items.label: V32AC
items.desc: Answering pattern of a V.32/V.32bis terminal.

items.label: V8bISeg
items.desc: First segment of initiating V.8 bis signal.

items.label: V8bRSeg
items.desc: First segment of responding V.8 bis signal.

items.label: ANS / CED
items.desc: V.25 answer tone, also T.30 called tone (2100 Hz).

items.label: /ANS / /CED
items.desc: Same tone after a phase reversal.

items.label: ANSam
items.desc: V.8 amplitude modified answer tone.

items.label: /ANSam
items.desc: ANSam after a phase reversal.

items.label: CNG
items.desc: T.30 calling tone (1100 Hz).

items.label: V.21 ch.1 '0'
items.desc: V.21 low channel, zero bit.

items.label: V.21 ch.1 '1'
items.desc: V.21 low channel, one bit. Also ESiSeg.

items.label: V.21 ch.2 '0'
items.desc: V.21 high channel, zero bit.

items.label: V.21 ch.2 '1'
items.desc: V.21 high channel, one bit. Also ESrSeg.

items.label: CT
items.desc: V.25 calling tone (1300 Hz).

items.label: ANS2225
items.desc: 2225-Hz indication for text telephony.

items.label: CI
items.desc: V.8 call indicator signal preamble.

items.label: V.21 preamble flag
items.desc: T.30 preamble of HDLC flags.

items.label: VBDGen
items.desc: Unidentified modem type.

items.label: V32AA
items.desc: Calling pattern of a V.32/V.32bis terminal.

viz.caption: THE PURE V.8 START-UP SEQUENCE (RFC 4734, SECTION 2.3)

messages.label: CI
messages.note: Repeated at least three times until ANSam is heard.

messages.label: CM
messages.note: Begins after a pause of at least half a second.

messages.label: JM
messages.note: Begins after two identical CM sequences.

messages.label: CJ
messages.note: Acknowledges JM; both sides then pause 75 ms and start the selected mode.
